sections.markdown:
## C2 — Confusable pairs and knowledge-graph hints: parking distances, passing rules, intersection and roundabout right of way
Confusable pairs among the parking distances, passing rules and right-of-way rules, each tied to one handbook page; hint metadata sits only in trailing lines.

FACT_ID: sec09-R01 | anchor: A02
The no-parking distance is 15 feet from a fire hydrant but 25 feet from the curb line of a cross street, and 15 feet from the right of way lines where there is no curb. [A02]
Why it matters: group parking distances; difficulty high; confusable fifteen versus twenty-five.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0058]

FACT_ID: sec09-R02 | anchor: A02
Near a fire or fire truck the parking buffer is one block inside city limits but 400 feet outside a city, while a parked car on a shoulder must be visible for 200 feet both ways. [A02]
Why it matters: group parking distances; difficulty high.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0058]

FACT_ID: sec09-R03 | anchor: A01
Passing clearance is at least two feet to the left of the passed vehicle, while the sight distance needed to pass on a curve or hill is at least 500 feet. [A01]
Why it matters: group passing; confusable clearance versus sight distance.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec09-R04 | anchor: A01
When passing, you signal your intention and blow the horn to alert the driver ahead; when being passed, you must help by moving to the right edge of the road if the passing driver blows the horn, and you must never increase your speed [A01].
Why it matters: group passing; confusable passer versus passed duties.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec09-R05 | anchor: A01
Passing on the right is generally illegal, but it is allowed on roads with two or more lanes each way, on one-way streets, beside a left-turning car, and from a right-turn lane. [A01]
Why it matters: group passing on right; misconception target.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0057]

FACT_ID: sec09-R06 | anchor: A03
At an uncontrolled intersection the car already inside goes first, and when two arrive together the car on the right goes first; facing cars split straight-versus-left, with the left turner waiting. [A03]
Why it matters: group right of way; difficulty high.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0059]

FACT_ID: sec09-R07 | anchor: A03
Having the right of way still requires you to slow down approaching the intersection and to avoid hitting anyone. [A03]
Why it matters: group right of way; misconception target.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0059]

FACT_ID: sec09-R08 | anchor: A04
In a traffic circle the vehicles already circulating have the right of way, and you exit only by turning right from the outside lane. [A04]
Why it matters: group circles; confusable with entering traffic.
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0060]

FACT_ID: sec09-R09 | anchor: A05
Entering roundabout traffic yields to vehicles and bicyclists already inside, while circulating traffic does not yield to approaching cars but does yield to pedestrians when exiting. [A05]
Why it matters: group roundabouts; difficulty medium.
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0061]

FACT_ID: sec09-R10 | anchor: A05
In a single-lane roundabout three-quarters of the way around replaces a left turn, while in a multi-lane roundabout the left lane is typically used for straight, left and U-turn movements. [A05]
Why it matters: group roundabouts; difficulty high.
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0061]

FACT_ID: sec09-R11 | anchor: A02
The backing speed limit of no more than 10 mph pairs with the rule to look over the right shoulder through the rear window, not just in the mirrors. [A02]
Why it matters: group backing; difficulty low.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0058]
